Skim the broth while simmering the bones for a clearer, cleaner flavor.
Add tamarind and fermented soybean paste gradually; the sweet-sour flavor should be gentle and should not overpower the shrimp and pork.
Briefly blanch fresh rice noodles if needed, drain them and pour on the broth just before serving.
Small river shrimp or small tiger shrimp

names: Vĩnh Châu Duck Curry Rice Noodles
fields: Tender duck and soft taro in golden curry fragrant with lemongrass and coconut milk; chewy rice noodles are served with bean sprouts and herbs.

Vĩnh Châu curry noodles combine rice noodles with duck cooked in curry, lemongrass and coconut milk. Bếp Việt adapts the local specialty documented by Soc Trang travel sources for a home pot, using Muscovy duck, taro and a moderate amount of curry seasoning.
Divide the noodles, duck and taro among bowls and ladle over the hot curry. Serve bean sprouts, herbs and lime separately.
Four bowls of rice noodles with duck curry in coconut milk and fresh accompaniments.
About 2 hours 20 minutes, including 30 minutes to marinate the duck.
Choose fresh Muscovy duck; clean it thoroughly and drain before marinating.
Marinate the duck for at least 30 minutes to infuse it with lemongrass and curry, then brown it before adding liquid.
Simmer gently so the meat softens without boiling the coconut milk over; add hot water if the curry becomes too thick.

names: Châu Đốc Xôi Xiêm Coconut Sticky Rice
fields: Glossy, tender sticky rice fragrant with coconut milk and pandan, served with lightly thickened palm-sugar egg sauce and optional durian.

Xôi Xiêm is a sweet snack associated with Châu Đốc, made with glutinous rice, coconut milk and, in some versions, pandan and durian. Bếp Việt adapts a home version served with an egg, palm-sugar and coconut sauce, cooked separately for easier control of its thickness.
Spoon the warm sticky rice onto plates, add sauce to taste and top with fresh durian if using. Serve promptly.
Four portions of coconut sticky rice served with palm-sugar egg sauce.
About 4 hours, including 3 hours to soak the rice.
Soak the glutinous rice for at least 3 hours and drain it so the grains steam evenly.
Stir the egg sauce continuously over low heat; do not let it boil hard or the egg may curdle.
Durian has a strong flavor; use a modest amount or omit it for a lighter coconut flavor.

names: Soc Trang Khmer Cốm Dẹp Flattened Rice
Khmer cốm dẹp for Ok Om Bok
fields: Soft, chewy flattened rice fragrant with young rice and fresh coconut, gently sweet and creamy.
Khmer cốm dẹp for Ok Om Bok

Cốm dẹp is a Khmer delicacy associated with Soc Trang and the Ok Om Bok festival. Young rice is pounded flat, then mixed with grated coconut, sugar and coconut water. Bếp Việt adapts a small-batch method and briefly rests the mixture so the grains soften and absorb the flavors.
Serve the flattened rice after mixing and resting for about 15 minutes. It may be placed on clean banana leaves or eaten with a spoon.
Four portions of flattened rice mixed with coconut, served after resting to soften.
About 25 minutes, including 15 minutes for the rice to soften.
how to make flattened rice with coconut
Use fresh, dry cốm dẹp from a reliable food source.
Add coconut water gradually; the grains should become soft and chewy without turning soggy.
Taste before adding all the sugar, since the rice and coconut vary in sweetness.

names: Hue steamed rice cakes with mung bean
fields: Soft white rice cakes with a slight dimple, topped with nutty mung beans, crisp bread and seaweed; served with a gently sweet vegetarian dip.
Hue steamed rice cakes with mung bean

Hue vegetarian bánh bèo is steamed in small cups and topped with mung beans cooked in annatto oil, crisp fried bread, sautéed leek and seaweed. Bếp Việt scales a home batch from the vegetarian topping described by Khám Phá Huế; serve with plant-based fish sauce or soy sauce.
Drizzle a little leek oil and dipping sauce over each cup, then add the seaweed just before eating to keep it crisp. Serve warm.
About 16 small cups of steamed rice cake, four per person, served as a snack or shared dish.
About 3 hours 20 minutes, including 2 hours to soak the mung beans; the batter-resting time overlaps with the soak.
Hue vegetarian banh beo rice cakes
Soak the mung beans until tender, steam and mash them before sautéing; the topping should be fluffy rather than wet.
Rest the batter for at least 30 minutes and stir again before pouring so the cakes steam evenly.
Preheat the cups in the steamer, keep the water at a vigorous boil and steam in small batches.
Use clearly labeled plant-based bánh mì and vegetarian fish sauce if preparing a fully vegan meal.

names: Hue bánh nậm with mung bean
fields: Thin, soft, smooth cakes with a golden, nutty mung-bean center and a light banana-leaf aroma; served with vegetarian soy sauce.
Hue bánh nậm with mung bean

Hue vegetarian bánh nậm are flat parcels of smooth white rice batter wrapped in banana leaves around mashed mung beans. Bếp Việt selects the mung-bean filling reported by VnExpress and scales the batter and steaming method for four; serve with soy sauce and chili.
Serve in the leaf or unwrap onto a plate. Dip in soy sauce with chili and eat warm.
About 12 small banana-leaf bánh nậm, three per person.
About 3 hours 20 minutes, including 2 hours to soak the mung beans; the beans can be soaked ahead.
Mash the mung beans into a cohesive paste with few hard pieces so it is easy to spread inside the thin cake.
Stir the batter constantly over low heat until thickened before spreading it on the leaves; a runny batter can spill over the edges.
Fold the leaves into flat parcels rather than making thick bundles so the batter cooks evenly.
Use banana leaves and soy sauce labeled as plant-based if preparing a fully vegan meal.
Small, chewy translucent cakes with a fragrant tofu and vegetable filling, served with savory-sweet soy sauce and optional chili.

Hue vegetarian bánh bột lọc have a chewy, translucent tapioca wrapper around tofu, wood-ear mushroom and carrot sautéed with leek. Bếp Việt follows the specific filling and method in VnExpress Cooking and the local technique described by Huế Ngày Nay; wrap in banana leaves, steam and serve with soy sauce.
Serve hot in their banana leaves with a small bowl of diluted soy sauce. Add fried leek if desired; avoid shrimp crackers for a fully vegan meal.
About 20 small banana-leaf tapioca cakes, five per person.
About 1 hour 20 minutes, including 15 minutes to soak the wood-ear mushrooms.
Press excess moisture from the tofu so the filling does not release water inside the parcel.
Sauté the carrot and wood-ear mushrooms first to remove their raw aroma, then season with tofu and leek.
Pour boiling water into the tapioca starch gradually, stirring as you go; knead only after the dough has cooled enough to handle.
Wrap the banana leaves securely and steam until translucent. If boiling unwrapped cakes, test one first to gauge the texture.

names: Hue bánh ít ram with vegetarian filling
fields: A golden crisp base supports a chewy sticky-rice dumpling filled with peppery tofu and vegetables; served with chili soy sauce.
Hue bánh ít ram with vegetarian filling

Vegetarian bánh ram ít pairs a soft, chewy glutinous-rice dumpling with a crisp base made from steamed and fried glutinous-rice dough. Bếp Việt uses tofu, wood-ear mushroom, carrot and leek, drawing on the plant-based fillings described by Huế Ngày Nay for Hue cakes. This is an editorial variation, not a claim that there is only one traditional filling.
Place the stuffed bánh ít on the ram base just before serving so the base stays crisp. Serve warm with vegetarian soy sauce.
About 12 pieces, each a soft stuffed sticky-rice cake on a crisp ram base, three per person.
About 1 hour 35 minutes, including 15 minutes for the dough to rest and the mushrooms to soak.
Divide the glutinous-rice dough between the plain ram bases and the stuffed bánh ít; cover unused dough with a damp towel so it does not dry out.
Cook the filling until dry before wrapping so the dumplings do not split during steaming.
Let the steamed bases cool and dry before frying for a crisper finish.
The tofu, wood-ear and carrot filling is Bếp Việt’s editorial choice; mashed mung beans can be used instead.

names: Hue bánh khoái with tofu and mushrooms
fields: Small golden-crisp pancakes filled with hot mushrooms and tofu and just-wilted bean sprouts, served with fresh greens, sour starfruit and vegetarian peanut-soy dip.
Hue bánh khoái with tofu and mushrooms

Hue vegetarian bánh khoái is a local vegetarian variation. Bếp Việt edits a small batch with a rice-and-wheat-flour batter, tofu, mushrooms, bean sprouts and leek; the dip uses fermented soy, peanuts and sesame instead of the meat-based broth sometimes served with bánh khoái.
Fold each pancake in half, cut into pieces and eat hot with mustard greens, lettuce, herbs, starfruit or green banana and vegetarian dipping sauce.
Eight small bánh khoái, two per person, served hot with greens and vegetarian peanut-soy dip.
About 1 hour 15 minutes, including 30 minutes for the batter to rest.
Rest the batter for about 30 minutes so the rice flour hydrates evenly; stir again before ladling it into the pan.
Cook the mushrooms and tofu until their moisture evaporates, then add the bean sprouts near the end so they stay crisp.
Use a small pan and moderately hot oil to crisp the edges without burning the pancake before the filling warms through.
Huế Ngày Nay confirms a vegetarian version but does not prescribe one filling; this tofu-and-mushroom filling is Bếp Việt’s editorial choice.
Tender chicken and lightly crisp wood ear mushrooms sit in a clear, softly set aspic with a gentle shiitake aroma.

Chicken is gently braised with pork rind and chicken feet to set the broth naturally, then combined with wood ear mushrooms, shiitake and black pepper. Once chilled, the clear aspic holds its shape. This is a familiar cold-weather and Tết dish in Northern Vietnam. Bếp Việt has scaled the home-style method to four servings.
Chill until fully set, then turn out onto a plate or spoon into portions. Serve cold with hot rice, pickled mustard greens or pickled scallions.
One medium bowl for four people, served with rice and pickled vegetables.
About 5 hours 55 minutes, including 80 minutes of cooking and 4 hours of chilling; it can be made a day ahead.
Blanch and rinse the bones, chicken feet and pork rind before simmering for a clearer broth.
Keep the simmer gentle and skim regularly; season lightly because cold food tastes more strongly seasoned.
Cool promptly in a shallow covered container, refrigerate, and do not leave at room temperature for an extended period.
Juicy, tender chicken with a light lotus-leaf fragrance, complemented by soft lotus seeds and aromatic shiitake.

Chicken is seasoned with shallot, garlic, fish sauce and pepper, wrapped in lotus leaves and steamed until cooked through. The leaves gently perfume the chicken while the steam keeps it moist. Bếp Việt includes lotus seeds and shiitake as optional additions for a family-style platter.
Open the lotus leaves while hot and spoon the steaming juices over the chicken. Serve at once with steamed rice and, if desired, lime-pepper salt.
One platter of steamed chicken for four, served with rice and vegetables.
About 75 minutes, including a 15-minute marinade and 35 minutes of steaming; actual steaming time depends on piece size.
Vietnamese chicken steamed in lotus leaves
Wipe the leaves clean and briefly blanch them so they soften and are less likely to tear when wrapped.
Cut the chicken through the joints and avoid splintering the bones; steam until the thickest pieces are fully cooked.
If the lotus leaves are small, overlap two leaves and place the folded seam underneath.

names: Hanoi Glass Noodles with Duck and Dried Bamboo Shoots
Hanoi duck and bamboo shoot vermicelli
fields: A clear, savoury broth with tender duck, fragrant bamboo shoots and springy glass noodles, finished with scallions and herbs.
Hanoi duck and bamboo shoot vermicelli

A Hanoi-style bowl combines tender ngan duck, chewy glass noodles and softened dried bamboo shoots in a clear duck broth. Bếp Việt follows the published home-cooking method and scales it to four portions; the dried shoots require an overnight soak and repeated boiling before cooking.
Place blanched glass noodles in warm bowls, add sliced duck and bamboo shoots, then ladle over the boiling broth. Finish with scallions, coriander and a squeeze of lime; serve chili on the side.
Four bowls of glass noodle soup with duck and dried bamboo shoots.
About 10 hours 10 minutes total, including an 8-hour soak for the dried bamboo shoots; active preparation and cooking take about 2 hours 10 minutes.
Vietnamese glass noodle soup with duck
Soak dried bamboo shoots overnight, then boil and rinse them more than once until tender and mild-smelling.
Simmer the duck gently and skim the broth; a rolling boil can make the stock cloudy.
Blanch the glass noodles separately just before serving so they do not become waterlogged in the stock.
Golden-brown duck pieces with lightly crisped skin, tender meat and an aromatic galangal-lemongrass coating.

Bone-in duck is marinated with fresh galangal, lemongrass and familiar Vietnamese seasonings, then browned and cooked until tender. The galangal-forward preparation appears on Hanoi duck menus; Bếp Việt adapts a published recipe for a four-person home meal and does not claim it is unique to the region.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a lightly dressed cucumber or blanched greens. Offer lime-pepper salt on the side if desired.
One platter of duck for four, served with rice and vegetables.
About 90 minutes total, including a 25-minute marinade and about 40 minutes of cooking; timing varies with the size of the pieces.
Use a heavy pan and brown the duck in batches so it sears instead of steaming.
Slice the galangal thinly or pound it coarsely so its aroma infuses the duck without overwhelming the meat.
Cook bone-in duck fully until tender; add small splashes of hot water if the pan dries before the pieces soften.

names: Goose braised with galangal and fermented rice
fields: Tender goose with lightly charred skin in a thick, fragrant sauce of galangal, lemongrass, fermented rice and shrimp paste.
Goose braised with galangal and fermented rice

Goose is briefly charred, then marinated with galangal, lemongrass, fermented rice and shrimp paste before being braised until tender. Hanoi catering and restaurant menus document goose prepared giả cầy; the listing is evidence that the dish is served locally, not proof that it is exclusive to Hanoi. Bếp Việt has adapted the method to a four-person household pot.
Serve hot with steamed rice or fresh rice noodles. Add herbs and sliced chili at the table; adjust the shrimp-paste aroma with lime if desired.
One pot of braised goose for four, served with rice or rice noodles.
About 1 hour 55 minutes total, including 20 minutes of marinating and about 65 minutes of cooking; larger pieces may need longer.
Char the skin lightly rather than burning it; wipe away soot before cutting the goose into pieces.
Use fermented rice and shrimp paste sparingly at first, then adjust after the sauce has simmered.
Keep the braise at a gentle simmer and add hot water in small amounts if the pot reduces before the goose is tender.

names: Phu Yen Boiled Cai Troi Greens with Fermented Fish Sauce
Boiled cai troi with mam cai
Phu Yen wild greens with fermented fish dip
fields: Just-tender greens with soft-crisp stems and deep green leaves, served beside a fragrant, savory bowl of mam cai with optional fresh chili.
Boiled cai troi with mam cai
Phu Yen wild greens with fermented fish dip

Cai troi grows around the hills and fields of Phu Yen. Local accounts describe briefly boiling the greens and dipping them in mam cai, a fermented fish sauce. Bep Viet standardizes the washing and four-person quantities while keeping the quick-cooking method so the greens retain their delicate aroma.
Drain the greens and arrange them on a plate. Serve warm or just cooled with a separate bowl of mam cai and steamed rice.
One shared side dish of greens for four people; seasonal wild greens shrink considerably when boiled.
About 20 minutes; washing and picking time depends on how tender and sandy the greens are.
Use cai troi only when its identity is confirmed by a trusted seller or knowledgeable forager; do not eat unidentified wild plants.
Wash several times, especially around the roots and leaf folds, to remove grit.
Add the greens to vigorously boiling water and remove as soon as tender; prolonged cooking dulls their characteristic aroma.
Taste the mam cai before adding anything because its saltiness and texture vary by maker.

names: Quick-Boiled Chua Le Greens from Phu Yen
fields: Barely tender leaves and fine stems that remain pleasantly crisp, with a light natural sourness.

Chua le is a seasonal wild green gathered around the hills of Phu Yen during the rainy season. Local cooks add it to already-boiling water and lift it out as soon as the water comes back to a boil, preserving the stems' crisp texture and mild tartness. Bep Viet edits the household quantity for four and does not assign a regional dipping sauce that the source does not document.
Drain well and serve as a vegetable side with rice. A familiar household dipping sauce may be served separately if desired.
One seasonal plate of greens for four people; the small leaves shrink substantially when cooked.
About 18 minutes; picking can take longer because the greens are small and often gritty.
Use only greens positively identified by a knowledgeable seller or forager and collected away from sprayed areas; never eat unidentified wild plants.
Soak briefly so grit settles, then rinse gently several times because the greens grow close to the ground.
Boil small handfuls in vigorously boiling water and lift them out as soon as the water returns to a boil.
The small greens lose considerable volume; prepare more raw greens than for a typical side dish.

names: Thai Nguyen Boiled Bo May Greens with Sesame Salt
Thai Nguyen dang cay greens with sesame salt
fields: Tender, vivid greens with a gentle bitter edge, paired with nutty toasted sesame crushed with salt.
Thai Nguyen dang cay greens with sesame salt

Bo may, also called dang cay, is remembered in Thai Nguyen as a seasonal wild green with a pleasantly bitter taste. Local reporting describes boiling the young shoots and leaves and eating them with sesame salt. Bep Viet edits a practical four-person home preparation while retaining this documented pairing.
Drain the greens and place them on a shared plate. Serve with a small bowl of freshly crushed sesame salt and steamed rice.
One shared plate of young greens and a small bowl of sesame salt for four people.
About 22 minutes, including picking, washing and preparing the sesame salt.
Buy bo may from a trusted local source that can identify it; do not substitute an unidentified wild plant.
Use young shoots and leaves, which cook quickly and have a more tender texture.
Toast sesame over low heat until aromatic, then cool before crushing so it stays nutty rather than scorched.
Keep the sesame salt lightly seasoned so the greens' characteristic bitterness remains noticeable.

names: Dien Bien Sweet Bamboo Shoots with Cham Cheo
Boiled sweet bamboo shoots with cham cheo
fields: Tender ivory bamboo shoots with a mild sweetness, served beside a rustic, fragrant, spicy-salty cham cheo with fresh herbs.
Boiled sweet bamboo shoots with cham cheo

Boiled sweet bamboo shoots are part of Thai home meals in the Northwest and are served with fresh cham cheo. Regional reporting describes the dip with salt, chili, garlic, aromatic herbs and either mac khen or doi seed. Bep Viet sets home quantities and a safe boiling method; the dip ratio is an editorial adaptation, not a single canonical recipe.
Drain the shoots and arrange on a plate. Serve cham cheo in a separate bowl for dipping while the shoots are warm.
One shared plate of boiled bamboo shoots with a small bowl of fresh cham cheo for four people.
About 50 minutes; thicker or more pungent shoots may need longer boiling or a change of water.
Choose fresh, sweet bamboo shoots from a reliable seller and remove all tough outer sheaths.
Bamboo shoots must be thoroughly cooked; if they remain bitter or pungent, change the water and continue boiling.
Toast mac khen briefly over low heat before crushing to release its aroma; use either mac khen or doi seed, not both unless desired.
Add the herbs after crushing the salt, chili, garlic and spice so their fresh fragrance remains.

names: Boiled Black Bean Shoots with Garlic Fish Sauce
Young bean shoots with garlic fish sauce
fields: Soft, tender leaves and stems with a mild nutty sweetness, paired with a balanced, garlicky, lightly sour and spicy fish sauce.
Young bean shoots with garlic fish sauce

Young black bean shoots are a thrifty home vegetable: the tender tips removed while growing beans can be boiled and dipped in tangy, spicy garlic fish sauce. Dak Lak reporting describes their nutty-sweet flavor and this simple preparation. Bep Viet edits the four-person quantities and balances the dip to household taste without assigning the dish to a specific province.
Drain the shoots well and serve on a plate with a separate bowl of garlic fish sauce and hot rice.
One shared plate of young black bean shoots with a bowl of dipping sauce for four people.
About 18 minutes; picking takes longer when the shoots include many tough stems.
bean shoots with garlic fish sauce
Buy shoots positively identified as black bean from a trusted grower; do not use leaves from unfamiliar bean plants.
Wash gently and remove tough stems without bruising the leaves.
Boil only until the stems are tender, then drain promptly to avoid limp, discolored greens.
Mix the fish sauce separately and season gradually so it complements rather than overwhelms the beans' mild flavor.
Golden-brown skin and juicy meat carry a light, creamy sweetness from the durian without masking the chicken.

Chicken is marinated with ripe durian flesh and roasted until fragrant and golden, with gentle fruity richness. The dish is associated with the orchard area of Lai Thieu, Binh Duong; Bếp Việt standardizes the proportions for a family meal.
Rest for 8 minutes before carving. Serve with sticky or steamed rice, cucumber and herbs.
One roasted chicken, carved to share among four people.
About 3 hours 25 minutes, including a 2-hour marinade; roasting time depends on the chicken and equipment.
Choose fragrant ripe durian and remove the seeds before mashing.
Marinate in the refrigerator; do not leave raw poultry at room temperature.
Use steady medium-hot coals and turn regularly so the durian does not burn; the thickest part should reach 74°C.

names: Chicken steamed in a Tan Trieu pomelo
fields: Tender, juicy chicken scented with pomelo oils and a faintly bitter, fresh finish.
Chicken steamed in a Tan Trieu pomelo

Seasoned chicken is placed inside a hollowed Tan Trieu pomelo and steamed with pomelo leaves. The steam carries the aroma of the rind into the meat, making this a distinctive dish of the Tan Trieu pomelo-growing area in Dong Nai.
Serve hot with lime-pepper salt or ginger fish sauce, fresh vegetables and steamed rice.
Free-range chicken steamed in a pomelo shell, shared by four people.
About 1 hour 50 minutes, including a 30-minute marinade; steam for 35–45 minutes depending on the pieces.
Choose a ripe but firm pomelo with a thick, unbroken rind; hollow it carefully.
Use pomelo leaves sparingly and avoid over-steaming, since the essential oils can turn bitter.
Arrange the chicken loosely so steam can circulate; the thickest part should reach 74°C.

names: Long Khanh Chicken and Salted-Fish Rice
Long Khanh chicken and salted-fish fried rice
Dong Nai chicken and salted-fish rice
fields: Separate grains fragrant with salted fish and aromatics, with soft shredded chicken and a balanced savory taste.
Long Khanh chicken and salted-fish fried rice
Dong Nai chicken and salted-fish rice

Cooled rice is stir-fried with shredded chicken and roasted, flaked salted fish. The combination makes a savory rice dish associated with Long Khanh, Dong Nai; Bếp Việt edits the proportions for a home meal.
Serve hot with cucumber, tomato or blanched greens.
One pan of chicken and salted-fish rice as a main dish for four.
About 1 hour 20 minutes if cooking fresh rice; less when pre-cooked rice is ready.
Long Khanh chicken salted fish rice
Dong Nai chicken salted fish fried rice
Cook the rice slightly dry and cool it completely; warm, moist rice can become sticky.
Salted fish can be very salty. Taste it before adding fish sauce or salt.
Stir-fry the fish and chicken first, then add the rice over fairly high heat; cook in batches if needed.

names: Mekong-Style Duck Stew with Green Peppercorns
Green peppercorn duck and potato stew
fields: Tender but intact duck pieces, potatoes steeped in a peppery broth, and fragrant green peppercorns.
Green peppercorn duck and potato stew

Duck is marinated, browned, then simmered with potatoes, lemongrass and green peppercorns until tender. The dish has been shared as part of Mekong Delta family feasts; this is Bếp Việt's home-style version.
Serve hot with steamed rice or bread, with fresh vegetables if desired.
One pot of green peppercorn duck and potatoes for four.
About 2 hours, including a 30-minute marinade; simmering time varies with the duck.
Rub duck with ginger and salt or a little rice wine to reduce odor, then rinse and pat dry.
Add potatoes after the duck has started to tenderize so they do not fall apart.
Add green peppercorns in two stages to retain some fresh aroma.

names: Mekong-Style Duck Braised in Coconut Water
fields: Tender duck infused with coconut water and seasoning, coated in glossy brown sauce with a balanced sweet-savory taste.

Duck is seasoned, browned, then gently braised in coconut water until tender and coated in a glossy reduction. This rustic method is commonly presented in Mekong Delta cooking; Bếp Việt adapts the seasoning for a family meal.
Serve hot with steamed rice, cucumber or fresh greens; spoon a little sauce over the rice.
One pot of coconut-braised duck to serve with rice for four.
About 1 hour 50 minutes, including a 30-minute marinade; braising time depends on piece size.
Clean the duck with ginger and salt, rinse thoroughly and pat dry.
Brown the skin side first so the duck renders fat and develops color; pour off excess fat if needed.
Braise over low heat and uncover near the end to reduce the sauce. Taste before reducing because both sauces are salty.

names: S’tiêng Bamboo-Tube Soup from Binh Phuoc
Bamboo-tube soup with young nhíp leaves and rattan shoots
fields: The nhíp leaves are soft, the rattan shoots retain a gentle bite and mild bitterness, and the buffalo skin is tender and chewy. The broth is lightly thickened and gently spicy.
Bamboo-tube soup with young nhíp leaves and rattan shoots

Canh thụt is a traditional S’tiêng dish made with young nhíp leaves, rattan shoots, buffalo skin and fresh chili. The ingredients are cooked with a little water in a bamboo tube and stirred with a bamboo stick. Bếp Việt keeps the ingredients and method recorded by the Binh Phuoc provincial portal, while editing the household quantities and offering a heatproof-pot adaptation.
Serve hot in a small pot or deep bowls with steamed rice. If cooking in a bamboo tube, keep it stable, leave the opening uncovered and never seal it.
One shared pot of soup for four people; Bếp Việt standardizes the quantities of nhíp leaves, rattan shoots and buffalo skin for home cooking.
About 60 minutes when using pre-tenderized buffalo skin; this excludes preparation of raw buffalo skin.
nhíp leaves and rattan shoots soup
Use only nhíp leaves and rattan shoots that are confidently identified, legally sourced and safely prepared; do not gather unidentified forest plants.
Buy cleaned, tenderized buffalo skin from a reliable food supplier; preparing raw buffalo skin is not included in the recipe time.
The local source records cooking in a bamboo tube and stirring with a bamboo stick; a heatproof pot is Bếp Việt’s home-kitchen adaptation.
Season lightly to preserve the natural bitter, nutty notes, and adjust the chili at the end.

names: Bù Gia Mập Fermented Móp Greens
fields: The shoots turn green-gold, stay crisp and taste mildly sour and salty, with no unusual odor, mold or slime.

Young móp shoots are a familiar wild vegetable in the Bù Gia Mập area. Dân Việt reports that sour-pickled móp is a common local preparation in Binh Phuoc. Bếp Việt standardizes the salt quantity and small-batch method; the crisp, tangy flavor develops over roughly two to three days, depending on room temperature.
Take out only what you need, drain and serve as a rice accompaniment. Garlic and fresh chili can be added after fermentation; refrigerate the remaining greens in a clean jar.
One small jar of pickled greens for four people; the finished yield depends on the tenderness of the shoots and how much liquid they release.
About 2–3 days to ferment; monitor the sourness and refrigerate when it reaches the desired flavor.
Use only móp greens that have been confidently identified, legally harvested and sold by a reliable food supplier; do not gather unidentified wild greens.
Use a clean jar, scald it with boiling water and let it dry. Keep the shoots fully submerged in brine to reduce spoilage risk.
The brine ratio is Bếp Việt’s starting point for a home batch; fermentation time changes with room temperature.
Discard the batch if mold, slime or an unusual smell appears. Once it tastes as sour as you like, refrigerate and use clean utensils.
The fish smells of charcoal, has lightly charred skin and firm, rich flesh; its own flavor remains at the center without a heavy seasoning crust.

Cá niên lives in the mountain streams of Quang Ngai, including the Tra Bong and Son Tay areas. The provincial broadcaster identifies simple charcoal grilling as a standout preparation because it preserves the fish’s natural flavor. Bếp Việt edits the household portion, cleaning steps and green-chili salt accompaniment.
Serve hot with green-chili salt, fresh herbs or other seasonal greens, and steamed rice. Choose fish from a legal source and favor responsible aquaculture or sustainable catch.
About 800 g of small fish as a shared main dish for four; wild cá niên can be seasonal and difficult to find.
About 38 minutes, excluding the time needed to heat the charcoal; larger fish take longer.
Wild cá niên is limited in supply. Avoid fish with unclear origins or very small fish; choose a legal, responsible source.
Clean the fish thoroughly and pat it dry before grilling so the surface does not steam and the flesh cooks evenly.
The local source describes a simple charcoal-grilled preparation with little seasoning; use only a light touch of salt and serve extra green-chili salt on the side.
Grill over steady glowing coals and turn gently to avoid excessive charring.

names: Sơn Tây Stream Goby Braised with Pepper
Quang Ngai stream goby pepper braise
Sơn Tây stream goby braised in caramelized sauce
fields: The fish is firm and coated in a glossy brown sauce, with balanced savory-sweet flavor and clear pepper aroma; the sauce is lightly reduced for rice.
Quang Ngai stream goby pepper braise
Sơn Tây stream goby braised in caramelized sauce

Small stream gobies from the Quang Ngai highlands are described by local residents as fragrant and pleasantly firm. People in Sơn Mùa, Sơn Tây, say they braise the fish with pepper or wild chili to eat with rice. Bếp Việt edits the fish-sauce ratio and a little caramel sauce for a four-person home meal; this is not presented as the only local method.

Serve in a small clay pot or deep plate, finish with freshly ground pepper and eat with hot rice and boiled greens. If stream goby is unavailable, use small goby from a farmed or legally sourced supply.
One small pot of braised fish to serve with rice for four; Bếp Việt standardizes the quantity from a family dish in the Quang Ngai highlands.
About 60 minutes including a 10-minute marinade; larger fish or a thick clay pot may need more time.
Wild stream gobies from the highlands are caught in limited quantities; use a legal source and avoid fishing in protected areas or seasons.

The pigeon is browned but not dry, the Vietnamese coriander remains fragrant and the seasoning is balanced; the crackers stay crisp at serving.

Minced pigeon is quickly stir-fried with shallots, garlic, chili, onion and Vietnamese coriander. Crisp shrimp crackers scoop up the aromatic, tender meat; Bếp Việt uses boneless meat for a family-friendly version.
Serve the hot pigeon mixture in a shallow bowl, topped with roasted peanuts and fried shallots. Keep the fried crackers separate for scooping.
One platter of minced pigeon with shrimp crackers, enough for four as an appetizer or snack.
About 45 minutes including cleaning, deboning and quick stir-frying.
chim cau bam xuc phong tom
Remove all small bones and mince the meat separately; do not mince bones into the dish.
Stir-fry over high heat and work in batches if needed so the meat browns instead of stewing.
Add Vietnamese coriander and scallions at the end and toss briefly to preserve their aroma.
Fry the shrimp crackers in properly heated oil and drain before serving.

names: Duck Stewed with Green Bananas and Tofu
Duck with green banana and tofu stew
fields: The duck is tender but not falling apart, the bananas are soft and intact, and the golden tofu has absorbed the lightly thickened broth.
Duck with green banana and tofu stew

Duck is marinated with ginger, lemongrass and simple seasonings, then simmered until tender with green bananas and golden fried tofu. The bananas turn mellow, the tofu absorbs the savory broth and the duck stays aromatic.
Serve hot with steamed rice or fresh rice vermicelli, making sure each portion includes duck, banana and tofu.
About 1.2 kg of duck stewed with green bananas and tofu, serving four.
About 115 minutes including 30 minutes of marinating; older duck or larger pieces may need longer simmering.
Duck Stewed with Green Bananas and Tofu
Rub the duck with ginger and rice wine, rinse and pat dry to reduce its strong aroma.
After peeling, soak the green bananas in lightly salted water to limit discoloration.
Simmer the duck until nearly tender before adding bananas; add tofu near the end to keep it intact.
Once the bananas are added, simmer gently and stir carefully.

names: Chicken Soup with White Beans and Taro
Chicken soup with fresh white beans and taro
White bean and taro chicken soup
fields: The chicken is tender, the white beans soft but intact and the taro mellow without dissolving; the light broth is fragrant with scallion and sawtooth coriander.
Chicken soup with fresh white beans and taro
White bean and taro chicken soup
Chicken thigh is lightly seared, then simmered with fresh white beans and taro until tender. The broth is mild and savory, while the beans and taro make this an easy, nourishing family soup.
Serve hot with chopped scallion and sawtooth coriander, alongside steamed rice. Adjust the seasoning at the end to keep the broth gentle.
A soup pot with 500 g chicken thigh, fresh white beans and taro, serving four.
About 80 minutes including 15 minutes of marinating; fresh white beans keep the cooking time shorter.
canh ga dau trang khoai mon
Chicken Soup with White Beans and Taro
Use fresh white beans; if substituting dried beans, soak and pre-cook them until tender first.
Sear the chicken briefly to firm its surface; it does not need to brown deeply.
Cut the taro into even pieces and stir gently to keep it intact.
Skim the broth early and season gradually.

names: Thai Nguyen Nham with Black Canarium
ingredients: Úc Kỳ fermented rice soy sauce
fields: The canarium remains soft but intact, with fragrant grilled fish and pork, lightly crisp banana stem, and a balanced savory-tart dressing.
Thai Nguyen Nham with Black Canarium

A Ha Chau specialty combining softened black canarium, fully cooked grilled carp, grilled pork belly, young banana stem, coconut, sour starfruit and aromatic leaves. Bếp Việt edits this version to use thoroughly cooked fish and a measured amount of fermented rice soy sauce for a balanced nutty, tangy and herbal flavor.
Serve on a platter with toasted rice crackers or nhội and fig leaves; offer extra Úc Kỳ fermented rice soy sauce on the side.
Four portions served with rice crackers or nhội leaves as a mixed dish for a family meal.
About 70 minutes; simmering and grilling times vary with ingredient size.
Úc Kỳ fermented rice soy sauce
Simmer the canarium gently until tender before removing the pits so the flesh stays intact.
Grill the carp and pork until fully cooked; cool slightly before flaking and mixing.
Add the fermented soy sauce and vinegar gradually to preserve the canarium’s nutty flavor.

names: Mekong Delta Linh Fish in a Light Broth
fields: The fish is tender but intact in a clear, lightly salty broth fragrant with pepper and shallot, served with crisp greens.
Mekong Delta Linh Fish in a Light Broth

Linh fish is gently braised in a lightly seasoned broth with a little pork fat, pepper and shallot, preserving the fish’s natural sweetness. It is commonly enjoyed with rice and seasonal field vegetables such as water lily stems, bean sprouts, sesbania flowers and herbs.
Serve in a clay pot or deep platter with hot rice, water lily stems, bean sprouts, sesbania flowers, herbs and lime.
Four portions served with steamed rice and a platter of Mekong Delta greens.
About 70 minutes including 10 minutes of marinating; braising time depends on fish size.
Use fresh linh fish and clean it gently to avoid bruising.
Once the pot simmers, lower the heat and gently shake the pot instead of stirring.
Season lightly at first and adjust near the end because fish sauce varies in saltiness.

names: Rạch Gốc Ba Khía Tamarind Stir-Fry
Cà Mau Ba Khía with Tamarind
Rạch Gốc Ba Khía in Tamarind Sauce
fields: The ba khía is fully cooked and firm, evenly coated in a glossy tamarind sauce with balanced sour-sweet-salty flavor and fragrant garlic.
Cà Mau Ba Khía with Tamarind
Rạch Gốc Ba Khía in Tamarind Sauce

Cleaned ba khía crabs are stir-fried until cooked through, then coated in a tamarind, garlic and chili glaze. The tangy sauce clings to the claws, shells and roe. Bếp Việt balances the sweet, salty and sour notes for rice or a casual shared plate.
Finish with scallions and Vietnamese coriander. Serve hot with steamed rice or bread, with a crab pick for the claws.
Four portions as a shared snack or a savory dish for a family meal.
About 45 minutes; cleaning time depends on whether the crabs are pre-cleaned.
Choose fresh, intact ba khía and scrub mud from the shell and claws.
Cook the crabs thoroughly; never taste uncooked sauce that has touched raw seafood.
Taste the crabs before adding fish sauce because some may already be salted.

names: Ninh Bình Fully Cooked Goat with Lime
Goat with Lime, Lemongrass and Sesame
fields: The goat is tender and fully cooked with no pink center; lime is bright but gentle, lemongrass and galangal are balanced, and toasted sesame adds nuttiness.
Goat with Lime, Lemongrass and Sesame

A Ninh Bình mountain-goat specialty traditionally made by steaming the goat until cooked, then tossing it with lime juice, lemongrass, galangal and toasted sesame. Bếp Việt keeps the familiar “tái chanh” dish name but provides a fully cooked version with no raw or pink meat.
Serve with fig leaves, Vietnamese balm, fresh herbs and thinly sliced green banana; dip in fermented soybean sauce or ginger fish sauce.
Four portions served with herbs, fig leaves, green banana and fermented soybean dip.
About 85 minutes including 20 minutes of marinating; steam the goat thoroughly before adding lime.
“Tái chanh” is the traditional dish name; this Bếp Việt version steams the meat fully.
Check the thickest center with a food thermometer. USDA recommends at least 63C for whole cuts of goat; this recipe targets about 71C for a well-done result.
Add lime only after the goat is cooked; citrus does not replace cooking.
The outside is lightly golden while the inside is opaque, moist and firm; galangal and lemongrass are fragrant and the fermented rice adds mild acidity.

Fresh sturgeon from the Suối Kẹm area of La Bằng is prepared in several local dishes, including grilled sturgeon. This Bếp Việt version marinates the fish with galangal, fermented rice, lemongrass and a little fish sauce, then grills it until opaque, fragrant and moist.
Serve hot with lettuce, lá lốt, perilla, sour starfruit and green banana; offer salt-chili dip or a light fish sauce dip.
Four portions served with fresh herbs, wrap vegetables and dipping sauce.
About 100 minutes including 40 minutes of marinating; grilling time varies with thickness and equipment.
sturgeon grilled with galangal and fermented rice
Clean the slime with warm water and salt; avoid boiling water that can damage the fish surface.
Cut evenly thick pieces so they cook at the same rate; avoid over-grilling.
Marinate under refrigeration and discard any marinade that touched raw fish rather than serving it as a dip.

names: Vĩnh Long Crispy Whole Elephant Ear Fish
fields: The whole fish is golden and evenly crisp, with puffed scales; the flesh is moist, firm and fragrant rather than dry or burnt.

The elephant ear fish is cleaned but left scaled, then deep-fried until the scales puff and crisp while the flesh stays tender. A signature Vĩnh Long dish, it is shared by wrapping the fish with rice paper, vermicelli, fresh herbs, starfruit and green banana.
Place the fish on a large platter. Pick off the flesh and wrap it with rice paper, vermicelli, herbs, starfruit and green banana. Serve with a sweet-sour garlic-chili fish sauce dip.
One fish of about 1 kg, served with greens, rice vermicelli and rice paper for four people.
About 70 minutes including a 15-minute salt-water soak; frying time depends on the fish size and oil temperature.
Fresh herbs, starfruit and green banana
Dry the fish thoroughly before frying to reduce splattering.
Use a deep pot and enough oil to submerge the fish; lower it in slowly once the oil is hot, then keep the heat moderate so it cooks through.
Use a food thermometer to check that the thickest flesh reaches at least 63°C; let the fish rest for about 3 minutes before serving.

names: Buôn Ma Thuột Beef with Tamarind Sauce
Buôn Ma Thuột beef dipped in tamarind sauce
fields: The tamarind sauce is lightly thick and balanced between sweet and sour; quickly dipped beef stays tender and the onion is softened but still crisp.
Buôn Ma Thuột beef dipped in tamarind sauce

Thin slices of beef are dipped in a gently bubbling, sweet-sour tamarind sauce with onion and a little butter. The Buôn Ma Thuột serving style keeps the beef tender and fragrant; greens and bread balance the rich sauce.

Set the hot pan of sauce in the middle of the table, with raw sliced beef on one side and watercress and bread on another. Dip a few slices at a time until just cooked; do not add all the beef at once.
Four portions of thinly sliced beef dipped in hot tamarind sauce, served with greens and bread.
About 60 minutes including 15 minutes to season the beef; dip each slice at the table to keep it tender.
Slice the beef across the grain; chilling it briefly makes even thin slices easier.
Taste the sauce before dipping because tamarind and fish sauce vary in acidity and saltiness.
Only bring out the amount of raw beef needed for each round; keep it separate from washed greens and cooked food.
The shrimp are firm, lightly crisp and coral pink; the starfruit is softened but still holds its shape, with gentle sourness coating the shrimp.

Small field shrimp are first roasted dry, then tossed with pork fat, shallots and sour starfruit. This rustic dish is nutty, lightly crisp and balanced between sour, salty and sweet, and is best served hot with white rice.
Spoon the shrimp and starfruit onto a plate, finish with scallions and pepper, and serve immediately with white rice and a light vegetable soup.
One plate of field shrimp with starfruit to share with rice among four people.
About 35 minutes; dry-roast the shrimp before frying the shallots and seasoning.
Drain the shrimp well before roasting so they dry quickly and splatter less.
Add the starfruit after the shrimp have firmed up so it does not collapse or release too much liquid.
Add fish sauce gradually because tiny shrimp absorb seasoning quickly.

names: Nam Ô Sour Reef-Fish Soup with Pineapple
Nam Ô sour fish soup with cá ong
fields: The broth is clear and lightly golden with a fresh sour finish; the cá căn stays firm and intact, and the pineapple and tomato remain in pieces.
Nam Ô sour fish soup with cá ong

Fresh cá căn is seasoned before cooking with pineapple, tomato and rice paddy herb. This Nam Ô fishing-village soup balances the firm sweetness of sea fish with the gentle sourness of pineapple and tomato and a touch of chili.
Ladle the fish and broth into a serving bowl, then finish with rice paddy herb and cilantro. Serve hot with steamed rice and optional chili fish sauce.
One sour soup pot with about 500 g of cá căn fish, served with rice for four people.
About 70 minutes including a 20-minute fish marinade; simmer gently so the fish does not break apart.
Nam O fish soup with pineapple
Choose fresh fish with clear eyes and firm flesh; clean it gently to avoid breaking the pieces.
Season the fish before adding it to gently boiling water, and avoid stirring so the pieces stay intact.
Adjust the sweet-sour seasoning after the fish is nearly cooked, as pineapple and tomato release liquid into the broth.

names: Yên Tử Bamboo Shoots Stir-Fried with Garlic
Yên Tử garlic bamboo shoot side dish
ingredients: Fish sauce or vegetarian soy sauce
fields: The bamboo shoots are cooked through but still crisp, lightly seasoned, with pale-golden fragrant garlic and fresh green scallions.
Yên Tử garlic bamboo shoot side dish

Yên Tử bamboo shoots are cleaned and thoroughly boiled before a quick stir-fry with garlic and scallions. The side dish is tender-crisp and fragrant, allowing the shoots' natural sweetness to stand out. This is a meat-free vegetable side, distinct from the existing Yên Tử bamboo shoots stir-fried with beef.
Serve hot as a separate vegetable side beside rice and a savory main. Use salt instead of fish sauce for a fully vegetarian meal.
One plate of garlic bamboo shoots as a vegetable side for four people.
About 110 minutes including a one-hour soak; thoroughly boil the shoots and change the water before stir-frying.
mang truc yen tu xao toi
Yen Tu bamboo shoots with garlic
Boil fresh bamboo shoots in plenty of water, changing the water and cooking them thoroughly before stir-frying; do not eat unprocessed fresh shoots.
Drain the shoots well before adding them to a hot pan so they stir-fry rather than steam.
Season with fish sauce for a regular meal or salt for a vegetarian meal; add scallions at the end to keep their color.
Fish sauce or vegetarian soy sauce

names: Hanoi-Style Vegetarian Tofu Dipped in Scallion Sauce
Fried tofu dipped in scallion soy sauce
fields: The tofu is lightly golden with a soft center, coated in green scallions and gently savory-sweet; the soy sauce forms a light coating rather than soaking in.
Fried tofu dipped in scallion soy sauce

A Bếp Việt plant-based version inspired by the old Hanoi technique of quickly dipping hot tofu into a seasoned scallion bowl. Golden fried tofu is dipped briefly in diluted soy sauce and scallions so it absorbs flavor while staying soft.
Serve hot with plain rice or mung bean porridge. Dip each piece as soon as it is fried so the scallions just wilt and the tofu stays hot.
Four portions of tofu served with rice or porridge as a side for a vegetarian family meal.
About 40 minutes, including 10 minutes to press the tofu; dip quickly while hot.
tofu dipped in scallion soy sauce
Fried tofu dipped in scallion sauce
Pat the tofu dry before frying to reduce splatter; fry in batches so the oil temperature does not drop.
Use a fully plant-based soy sauce; this version replaces the fish sauce and pork fat in the source description.
Dip both sides quickly, since soaking makes the tofu too salty and soft.

names: Northern Vietnamese Vegetarian Cà Bung Eggplant Stew
fields: The eggplant is tender but intact, the tofu is seasoned, and the pale golden broth is lightly thick with gentle sourness from fermented rice; perilla and lolot are aromatic.

A Bếp Việt plant-based version inspired by Northern cà bung: eggplant simmers with tomato, fermented rice, turmeric and herbs, with fried tofu for a nutty bite. It omits meat and shrimp paste and uses vegan soy sauce to keep the dish fully plant-based.
Ladle into a bowl or small clay pot while hot. Finish with scallions, perilla and lolot, and serve with plain rice or rice vermicelli.
Four portions of eggplant stewed with tofu, served with plain rice or rice vermicelli.
About 65 minutes, including a 20-minute eggplant soak; simmer gently until tender but not broken down.
vegetarian eggplant stew with fermented rice
Northern Vietnamese eggplant and tofu stew
Soak the eggplant in salted water with a little vinegar, then rinse and drain to reduce browning; stew until fully tender.
Use mature, pleasantly sour fermented rice and strain it; add seasoning gradually because acidity and saltiness vary.
Stir gently after adding eggplant so the pieces keep their shape; add the herbs at the end to preserve their aroma.

names: Northwest Vietnamese Luffa and Peanut Soup
fields: The broth is light and clear, the peanuts are soft with a little texture, and the green luffa is tender but not mushy; scallions and Vietnamese coriander smell fresh.

Luffa and peanut soup is a simple family dish recalled from a Northwest Vietnamese home kitchen. Crushed fresh peanuts are cooked first until soft and nutty, then luffa is added to keep its light sweetness. This Bếp Việt version uses plant-based oil and seasonings.
Ladle into a soup bowl and finish with scallions, Vietnamese coriander and a little pepper. Serve hot with plain rice; it is best just after cooking.
One pot of luffa and fresh peanut soup for four people to eat with rice.
About 40 minutes; cook the peanuts until tender before adding the luffa for the last few minutes.
Crush the peanuts moderately so they release their nutty flavor without making the broth too thick.
Cook the peanuts until tender before adding the luffa; the gourd cooks quickly, so simmer it only for the final few minutes.
Peanuts are a common allergen; tell guests clearly that the soup contains them.

names: Northern Vietnamese Quick-Pickled Mustard Greens and Radish
fields: The stalks are crisp, the leaves are yellow-green and the radish slices are translucent; the flavor is mildly salty and tart, without slime or off odors.

A cool-season Northern Vietnamese side dish of mustard leaves, stalks and radish lightly fermented in a mild salt-and-sugar brine until crisp, yellow-green and gently sour. This small-batch version is ready after about one day of mild fermentation.
Use clean chopsticks to take a small portion, drain it and serve with rice, tofu or a braised dish. Rinse briefly if it tastes too salty.
One small jar of quick-pickled mustard greens and radish as a side for four people over several meals.
About 24 hours 30 minutes, including one day of mild fermentation; it may sour sooner in a warm room.
Northern Vietnamese quick pickled mustard greens and radish
Use a clean glass or ceramic jar that has been scalded and dried; keep all vegetables fully submerged beneath the brine.
Check the flavor after 24 hours because warmer rooms ferment faster; refrigerate once it reaches the desired mild sourness.
Discard the whole jar if mold, stringy slime, a rotten smell or an unusual color appears; do not taste food that shows spoilage.

names: Northern Delta Stir-Fried Water Bamboo Shoots with Egg
Northern Vietnamese Water Bamboo Shoots with Egg
fields: The shoots are just tender and still crisp, the egg is softly set around them, and scallions and cilantro are fragrant; the plate is not watery.
Northern Vietnamese Water Bamboo Shoots with Egg

Thin slices of water bamboo shoots are quickly stir-fried with egg, shallot and herbs. This is a seasonal vegetable dish of the Northern Delta; the Bếp Việt version uses vegetable oil and salt instead of pork fat and fish sauce used in some preparations.
Serve hot with freshly cooked rice and finish with pepper. Avoid covering the plate for long so the shoots keep their crispness.
One plate of seasonal water bamboo shoots and egg for four people with rice.
About 25 minutes; stir-fry briefly and cook the egg fully.
Northern Delta stir fried water bamboo shoots with egg
Choose firm shoots with fresh sheaths; slice evenly and stir-fry over medium-high heat for a short time.
Add the egg when the shoots are just tender and stir until the egg is fully cooked.
This version uses oil and salt and contains egg; it is not vegan.

names: Hanoi Duck with Rice-Vinegar Broth and Herb Garnishes
Duck and dấm bỗng herb platter
fields: The duck is tender but intact; the broth is lightly sour with dấm bỗng and fragrant galangal; the fresh garnishes stay crisp.
Duck and dấm bỗng herb platter

Hanoi duck dấm ghém combines poached duck, pork belly, omelet and Vietnamese pork roll with a galangal and dấm bỗng broth, banana blossom, bean sprouts and herbs. This smaller Bếp Việt home version keeps the bright sour broth and fresh, build-your-own garnishes.

Arrange the duck, pork belly, omelet and pork roll with vermicelli, banana blossom, bean sprouts, herbs and pickled shallots. Ladle hot broth into bowls; add a little lime shrimp paste dip if desired.
A shared platter of duck, vermicelli and herb garnishes for four people.
About 130 minutes including a 15-minute seasoning rest; simmering time depends on the duck pieces.
Briefly blanch the duck and bones, then rinse the pot for a clearer, cleaner broth.
Add dấm bỗng near the end and adjust gradually because its acidity varies by batch.
Keep raw poultry away from ready-to-eat garnishes; chill leftovers within two hours.

names: Duck steamed with young lotus buds
fields: The duck is tender with a delicate lotus aroma; the buds are soft, gently sweet and still hold their shape.
Duck steamed with young lotus buds

Liên áp, duck steamed with young lotus buds, appears in Tản Đà thực phẩm (1943). The recorded method lightly seasons chopped duck with fish sauce and salt, then steams it over the buds for more than an hour. This home adaptation keeps the seasoning restrained so the softened lotus can be eaten with the duck.
Arrange the cooked lotus buds as a bed and place the hot duck on top. Serve with plain rice or wrap the duck in young lotus leaf and dip in mild ginger fish sauce.
Chopped duck steamed with young lotus buds as a main dish for four.
About 105 minutes including a 10-minute seasoning rest; steaming takes over an hour depending on piece size.
Choose closed, young lotus buds without bruises; rinse carefully and drain before steaming.
Keep the seasoning light to preserve the lotus aroma; bring the steamer water to a boil first.
Use a food thermometer to check that the thickest piece reaches at least 74°C; do not let the steamer run dry.

names: Hanoi Sweet-and-Sour Mixed Noodles with Muscovy Duck
ingredients: Vietnamese mint and rice paddy herb
fields: Loose vermicelli is lightly coated in a balanced sweet-sour dressing; the duck is firm and juicy, bamboo shoots crisp, and herbs and peanuts fresh.

Sweet-and-sour mixed duck vermicelli is a Hanoi way of serving bún ngan: vermicelli and sliced duck are tossed with sour bamboo shoots, Vietnamese mint, peanuts and a sweet-sour dressing, with broth on the side. Bếp Việt cooks duck and offal thoroughly and tosses the noodles just before serving.
Toss the vermicelli with just enough dressing. Top with duck, gizzard, liver, sour bamboo shoots and herbs; finish with peanuts and fried shallots. Serve at once with hot broth.
Rice vermicelli tossed with Muscovy duck, sour bamboo shoots, peanuts and herbs for four.
About 115 minutes including a 20-minute rest; the duck can be poached ahead and noodles tossed when serving.
Mixed vermicelli with broth on the side
Vietnamese mint and rice paddy herb
Blanch and taste the sour bamboo shoots first; if too salty or sharp, boil and rinse them.
Poach the duck gently and skim the broth; check that both meat and offal reach at least 74°C.
Keep dressing away from raw duck and toss the noodles just before serving so they do not soften.

names: Sông Cầu Grilled Chicken, Phú Yên
fields: The skin is golden brown with a few fragrant charred spots; the meat is cooked through, juicy and moderately seasoned.

Sông Cầu grilled chicken is recognized as a specialty associated with Sông Cầu, Phú Yên. Bếp Việt butterflies a free-range chicken, seasons it with fish sauce, onion, garlic and pepper, then grills it slowly for browned skin and juicy meat. The home seasoning and timing are editorial and do not represent one restaurant's recipe.
Carve the chicken into pieces and serve hot with lime-pepper salt, fresh greens and plain rice or sticky rice.
One butterflied free-range chicken with a dipping salt for four people.
About 95 minutes including a 30-minute marinade; grilling time depends on the oven, grill and chicken weight.
Butterfly and press the chicken flat for even heat; pat the skin dry before seasoning.
Grill on a rack over a tray so fat does not drip into the flame.
Check the thickest part of the thigh for at least 74°C; rest the chicken for 10 minutes before carving.
The patties are golden brown with lightly charred fragrant edges; the inside is moist, cohesive and fully cooked, with lemongrass and garlic aromas.

Vietnamese chả ngỗng nướng uses minced goose breast or thigh with a little fat to keep the patties tender. Lemongrass, garlic, shallot, pepper and honey brown fragrant on the grill. Bếp Việt's home recipe uses a thermometer to make sure the minced poultry cooks safely throughout.
Serve the patties hot on skewers with fresh herbs, cucumber, rice or vermicelli. Offer lime-pepper salt or sweet-sour fish sauce for dipping.
About twelve grilled goose patties, serving four people.
About 75 minutes including a 30-minute chilled rest; grilling time varies with patty size and equipment.
Choose goose thigh or breast with a little fat; mince it to a coarse paste so the patties stay juicy.
Rest the mixture in the refrigerator for 30 minutes so it binds and absorbs the seasoning.
Grill until the center of each patty reaches at least 74°C; do not rely on surface color alone.
The broth is clear with a gentle fish aroma; the noodles are soft yet chewy, with sweet steamed fish cake and fragrant fried fish cake.

A Quy Nhơn coastal specialty with clear fish-bone broth, tender-chewy bánh canh noodles and two kinds of fish cake. This home version uses fresh packaged noodles to simplify the work while keeping the local way of serving it hot with scallions, pepper and chili.
Divide the noodles among bowls, ladle over hot broth and arrange the fish cake on top. Finish with scallions, cilantro and fried shallots; serve with lemon and chili.
Four hot bowls of bánh canh, each topped with fried and steamed fish cake.
About 75 minutes; simmer the fish bones for 35–40 minutes and cook noodles separately to keep the broth clear.
Use fresh fish bones and heads; remove the gills and dark blood so the broth stays clear and mild.
Cook the bánh canh separately according to its package, then portion it into bowls so the broth does not turn cloudy or starchy.
If making fish cake from raw fish, steam or fry it until the center reaches at least 63°C; use a separate board and plate for raw fish.

names: Phan Thiết One-Sun-Dried Squid Grilled with Chili Salt
fields: The squid is firm, lightly charred and fragrant, opaque and tender inside; a thin layer of chili salt seasons without hiding its flavor.

Phan Thiết squid is dried in the sun once, so its surface is dry while the flesh stays supple and sweet. A quick chili-salt grill brings out its seaside flavor; this version balances the seasoning for a family meal.
Cut the squid on a diagonal and serve with lime and herbs. Eat hot with steamed rice or wrap in rice paper with greens.
One platter of grilled one-sun-dried squid to share among four people, with rice or greens.
About 35 minutes, including a 10-minute marinade; grill briefly on each side to keep the squid tender.
Phan Thiết one-sun squid grilled with chili salt
Choose one-sun squid from a traceable source and keep it chilled; thaw frozen squid overnight in the refrigerator.
Pat the squid dry before grilling to reduce splatter and help it brown evenly.
Grill until the thickest part is opaque and reaches 63°C; never reuse the plate that held raw squid.

names: Hàm Ninh Boiled Crab with Lime-Pepper Salt
Phú Quốc crab with lime-pepper salt
fields: The shells are bright red and the meat is opaque, firm and sweet; the dipping salt is tangy and peppery without overwhelming the crab.
Phú Quốc crab with lime-pepper salt
Hàm Ninh crab is prized for its sweet, firm meat. The simple local preparation boils fresh crab and serves it with lime-pepper salt, letting the seafood and fragrant Phú Quốc pepper stand out.
Arrange the hot crabs on a large platter with lime-pepper salt and herbs. Crack each crab as you eat and use a separate plate for shells.
Four portions of boiled crab, about one medium crab per person.
About 40 minutes; boil a few minutes longer for larger crab until the meat is firm and opaque.
Phú Quốc crab with lime pepper salt
Choose live crab with intact shells and keep it chilled; do not cook crab that was dead before cooking.
Scrub the shells and legs under cold running water; keep live crab away from herbs, lime and ready-to-eat food.
Boil until the shell is red and the meat is firm and opaque. Serve on a clean platter and refrigerate leftovers within two hours.

names: Phú Yên Tuna Eye Stewed with Chinese Herbs
Phú Yên tuna eye with Chinese herbs
fields: The tuna eye is tender but holds its shape, and the clear broth is gently fragrant with ginger and herbs, lightly savory with a sweet finish from the dates.
Phú Yên tuna eye with Chinese herbs

A Tuy Hòa specialty that uses the large eye from ocean tuna and gently stews it with an edible Chinese-herb soup packet, red dates, goji berries and ginger. The broth is aromatic and the flesh around the eye becomes rich and tender; this home recipe makes four small bowls and makes no medicinal claims.
Ladle an eye and broth into each warm clay bowl. Serve with perilla, scallions and bread or fresh rice noodles.
Four small bowls of stewed tuna eye, one serving per person.
About 85 minutes; gently steam for 50–60 minutes until tender and cooked through.
Phú Yên tuna eye stewed with Chinese herbs
Buy cleaned tuna eyes from a reputable seafood supplier, keep chilled and thaw in the refrigerator; discard anything with sour, ammonia-like or spoiled odors.
Use a food-grade herb soup packet with a labeled ingredient list, not an unidentified medicinal mixture.
Stew until the thickest flesh reaches 63°C and is tender; keep the knife, board and plate that touched raw tuna separate.

names: Sea-urchin patties with sesame rice cracker
fields: The patties are golden and fragrant, set through the center yet softly rich; pepper, scallions and fish sauce bring out the flavor of the sea.
Sea-urchin patties with sesame rice cracker

Chả nhum is a Phú Quốc sea specialty: fresh sea-urchin meat is beaten with scallions, pepper and fish sauce, then fried until golden. This home version forms small patties for easy turning and keeps the traditional sides of thick sesame rice cracker, fresh greens and green banana.
Arrange the hot patties on a plate and serve with sesame rice cracker, fresh greens and thinly sliced green banana. Eat as a savory rice-side dish or wrap in rice paper.
